questions.question: In a binary assignment model with 3 agents and 3 tasks, $x_{ij}=1$ if agent $i$ receives task $j$. Which constraint states that task 2 is carried out by exactly one agent?
An assignment problem pairs 4 agents with 4 tasks, each agent receiving exactly one task and each task exactly one agent. How many complete assignments are there?

In the binary assignment model, a planner wants the total execution time to be as small as possible, where $c_{ij}$ is the time agent $i$ needs for task $j$. What does the objective $\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}$ measure?
options: The sum of the execution times of the chosen pairs
The largest execution time among the chosen pairs
The smallest execution time among the chosen pairs
The sum of all $n^2$ times in the table

questions.question: An assignment problem pairs $n$ agents with $n$ tasks so that each agent receives exactly one task and each task exactly one agent. Which situation fits this definition directly?
options: Four workers share six jobs, each worker doing one job.
Two nurses cover five shifts, each nurse several shifts.
One truck visits four customers in the cheapest order.
Three machines go to three locations, one per location.

questions.question: The cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&8&4\\7&3&6\\2&9&5\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks, entry $(i,j)$ is the cost $c_{ij}$ of giving task $j$ to agent $i$) is given. What is the total cost of giving task 2 to agent 1, task 3 to agent 2 and task 1 to agent 3?
In a binary assignment model with 3 agents and 3 tasks ($x_{ij}=1$ if agent $i$ receives task $j$), a proposed solution has $x_{11}=x_{22}=x_{32}=1$ and all other $x_{ij}=0$. Why is it infeasible?
options: Agent 3 receives two tasks instead of one.
Agent 1 is left without any task in this solution.
It is feasible, as each agent has one task.
Task 2 is assigned twice and task 3 not at all.

questions.question: How many binary variables and how many equality constraints does the binary assignment model have for 5 agents and 5 tasks?
options: 5 variables and 5 equality constraints
25 variables and 10 equality constraints
25 variables and 5 equality constraints
120 variables and 10 equality constraints

questions.question: A solution of a 3-agent, 3-task binary assignment model is shown as the 0/1 table $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, where the entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $x_{ij}$ and $x_{ij}=1$ means agent $i$ receives task $j$. Which agent carries out task 1?
options: Agent 3
Agent 1
Agent 2
No agent

questions.question: For the cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&9\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks, entry $(i,j)$ is the cost $c_{ij}$ of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), why does letting each agent take its own cheapest task fail to solve the assignment problem?
options: Agent 1's cheapest task is too expensive for agent 2.
Taking the cheapest tasks always gives the optimum.
Both agents' cheapest choices are the same task.
The cheapest choices give the worst assignment.

questions.question: For $n$ agents, $n$ tasks and binary $x_{ij}$, suppose each $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ is replaced by $0\le x_{ij}\le1$, keeping $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ and $\sum_ix_{ij}=1$, with integer costs. Which statement about the relaxed model is correct?
options: Every optimal solution has all $x_{ij}$ in $\{0,1\}$.
It has an optimal solution with all $x_{ij}$ in $\{0,1\}$.
Its optimal value can be lower than the binary optimum.
The same holds for every binary integer program.

questions.question: A planner wants to assign $n$ agents to $n$ tasks one to one so that total profit $\sum_i\sum_jp_{ij}x_{ij}$ is as large as possible, where $p_{ij}$ is the profit of agent $i$ doing task $j$. How must the binary assignment model change?
options: The equations $=1$ become $\le1$ to allow higher profits.
Profits must first be converted into costs $M-p_{ij}$.
The variables become continuous so profits can be split.
Just the objective, now $\max\sum_i\sum_jp_{ij}x_{ij}$.

questions.question: For the cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}6&2&7\\4&5&3\\8&6&5\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks, entry $(i,j)$ is the cost $c_{ij}$ of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), what is the minimum total cost of a complete assignment?

For the cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}6&2&7\\4&5&3\\8&6&5\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks, entry $(i,j)$ is the cost $c_{ij}$ of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), the minimum total cost is 11, using entry $(1,2)$; the second-cheapest assignment costs 13 and also uses $(1,2)$. If $c_{12}$ rises from 2 to 7, what is the new minimum total cost?

For the cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3&8&5\\4&2&7\\6&5&1\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks, entry $(i,j)$ is the cost $c_{ij}$ of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), agent 2 must carry out task 1 (so $x_{21}=1$ is added to the model). What is the minimum total cost now?

In the binary assignment model with positive costs $c_{ij}$, suppose both families of equations are weakened to $\sum_jx_{ij}\le1$ and $\sum_ix_{ij}\le1$, and total cost is still to be made as small as possible. What would the optimal solution be?
options: All $x_{ij}=0$: nothing is assigned, at cost 0.
The same assignment, as $\le1$ is only a relaxation.
Each agent would take several cheap tasks.
The model would become infeasible.

questions.question: In the assignment model with constraints $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ for every agent $i$ and $\sum_ix_{ij}=1$ for every task $j$, suppose $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ is replaced by the weaker requirement that each $x_{ij}$ is a nonnegative integer. Does the set of feasible solutions change?
options: Yes; now $x_{ij}=2$ is allowed for some pair.
Yes; fractional assignments now become feasible.
No; the equations already force every $x_{ij}\le1$.
No; but only because the costs are positive.

questions.question: For the cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}6&4&3\\2&6&5\\8&5&9\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks, entry $(i,j)$ is the cost $c_{ij}$ of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), a planner proposes task 3 for agent 1, task 1 for agent 2 and task 2 for agent 3, at cost 10. Which argument proves this optimal without listing all six assignments?
options: Each agent pays its row minimum, and no assignment can cost less.
Each task gets its column minimum, so no assignment can cost less.
It uses the smallest entry of the matrix, 2, so it is optimal.
It avoids the largest entry of the matrix, 9, so it is optimal.

questions.question: Agent A must carry out exactly two of three tasks and agent B exactly one. A's costs for tasks 1, 2, 3 are 4, 6, 5 and B's are 3, 2, 7. The planner duplicates A's row to obtain a square assignment problem. What is the minimum total cost?
